title: FTC's AI-accuracy comment window closes July 31 — hidden output steering could count as Section 5 deception
subtitle: The proposed policy statement says AI companies that quietly steer models away from correct answers may violate federal consumer-protection law, while ordinary hallucinations remain outside its scope.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Federal Trade Commission's public comment period on its proposed AI-accuracy policy statement — formally, the Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems — closes on Friday, July 31, 2026. The statement was released on July 1, and its core position is that when an AI company steers a model's output away from a correct answer without telling users, that undisclosed steering can amount to deception under Section 5 of the FTC Act. Comments are filed at regulations.gov under docket FTC-2026-0859. The proposal originates from Executive Order 14365, signed December 11, 2025, on the national AI policy framework.

The line the FTC is drawing is narrower than critics have suggested. Ordinary AI mistakes — the wrong answers caused by real technical limits, commonly called hallucinations — are explicitly out of scope. What the statement targets is deliberate, undisclosed alteration of outputs: safety fine-tuning that a company markets as neutral accuracy, ideological guardrails presented as factual refusals, or commercial steering (product placement, competitor suppression) hidden inside the model's response. If enforced, the theory would push AI providers to disclose the categories of interventions applied to a model's outputs the same way food companies disclose ingredients — not the exact recipe, but the fact of the intervention.

This lands in the middle of a busy US regulatory month. The EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency rules become enforceable on August 2, 2026 with maximum penalties of €15 million or 3% of global turnover. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act SB315 was signed earlier in July. The FTC statement is smaller in scope but arguably more precedent-setting for the US market, because it maps AI behavior onto an existing, well-established federal deception standard rather than a new AI-specific regime. If it survives comments and litigation intact, it becomes the framework that all AI-facing US consumer products have to comply with by default, without new legislation.

For learners: the takeaway is a distinction worth carrying with you. A hallucination is a bug; a hidden intervention is a policy. The FTC's line separates the two, and it matters because the same wrong output can come from either cause and the responsibility is very different. When you evaluate any AI product — a chatbot, a search assistant, a coding tool — ask what the vendor discloses about the interventions applied to its outputs. The good actors will tell you; the ones that do not are betting no regulator will ever ask.
